title: Lottery Tax by State: What Winners Keep in 2026
description: Win $500M in Powerball? See exact take-home amounts after federal and state taxes in every state — the gap between best and worst is over $36 million.
content:
What This Article Calculates — and Why Your State Matters

If you won $500 million in Powerball tonight, here is exactly what you would take home in each state. Not a rough estimate. Not a ballpark. Specific dollar amounts, calculated from the lump sum cash value down through federal withholding, the top marginal rate, and every state's tax rate on lottery winnings.

The answer changes dramatically depending on where you live. Understanding lottery tax by state is not an abstract exercise — the difference between winning in New York versus Florida on a $500 million jackpot is more than $36 million in your pocket. That is real money, and it comes down entirely to your zip code on the day you claim your prize. Use our lottery tax calculator to run your own numbers with any jackpot size and your specific state.

Federal Tax Calculation: How the IRS Takes Its Cut First

Before your state touches a dollar, the federal government gets paid. Here is exactly how that works on a large jackpot.

Step 1: Immediate Federal Withholding

The IRS requires lottery operators to withhold 24% on prizes over $5,000 at the time of payment. On a $238 million lump sum (which is the approximate cash value of a $500 million advertised jackpot — roughly 60% of the headline number), that immediate withholding equals $57,120,000. You receive a check for approximately $180,880,000 that same day.

Step 2: The Tax Return Gap

That withholding does not close your federal tax bill. For single filers in 2026, the top federal marginal rate of 37% applies to income above $626,350. A $238 million lottery prize sits entirely in that bracket. The effective federal rate on the full lump sum is 37%, which equals $88,060,000 in total federal taxes. After subtracting the $57,120,000 already withheld, you owe an additional $30,940,000 when you file your return. This is the 13-percentage-point gap — the difference between the 24% withholding rate and the 37% rate that actually applies — that catches many winners off guard.

After federal taxes only, your $238 million lump sum becomes $149,940,000. What happens next depends entirely on your state.

Lump Sum vs. Annuity: Real Dollar Figures on a $500M Powerball Win

Winners face a second major decision before taxes even enter the picture: take the lump sum or accept the annuity paid over 29 years.

Lump Sum

The cash option on a $500 million Powerball jackpot is approximately $238 million. After federal taxes at 37%, that leaves $149,940,000 before state taxes. In a zero-tax state like Florida or Texas, that is your final number. In New York, state and city taxes reduce it further — down to approximately $125,000,000 for a New York City resident.

Annuity

The annuity pays the full $500 million over 29 annual installments, with payments increasing by 5% each year. The first payment is roughly $7.9 million; the final payment is approximately $30.5 million. Each payment is taxed as ordinary income in the year received — meaning the 37% federal rate applies to most payments, and your state taxes each check separately. The annuity's total post-tax value depends on your state, your longevity, and future tax law changes — which is why most financial advisors model both options before recommending one. For this article, all state-by-state comparisons use the $238 million lump sum as the baseline.

The difference between winning a $500M Powerball jackpot in New York City versus Florida is more than $36 million in after-tax cash — purely because of where you live when you claim the ticket.

Best and Worst States for Lottery Winners Ranked by Dollar Kept

The Best States: Keep the Full $149,940,000

Nine states levy zero tax on a $238 million lump sum, leaving winners with the maximum post-federal take-home of $149,940,000:

  • California — state law exempts lottery winnings from income tax. See California lottery taxes for full details.
  • Florida — no state income tax at all.
  • Texas — no state income tax.
  • Washington — no state income tax.
  • Wyoming — no state income tax.
  • South Dakota — no state income tax.
  • Tennessee — no state income tax.
  • New Hampshire — no state income tax on earned or prize income.
  • Pennsylvania — specifically exempts lottery winnings from the state's 3.07% income tax.

The Worst States: Where Taxes Hit Hardest

At the other end of the spectrum, New York lottery taxes represent the single heaviest burden in the country. New York State's rate of 10.9% on lottery winnings already costs winners $25,942,000 on a $238 million lump sum, reducing take-home to $123,998,000. New York City residents pay an additional 3.876% city income tax on top of that, pushing the combined state-plus-city rate to roughly 14.776% and the total state-and-city tax bill to approximately $34,968,000 — bringing the final take-home down to roughly $114,972,000.

New Jersey is close behind with a 10.75% state rate costing winners $25,585,000. Minnesota's 9.85% rate results in a $23,443,000 state bill. Oregon at 8.0% costs $19,040,000.

The gap between winning in a zero-tax state and winning as a New York City resident on this exact jackpot is $34,967,880 — money that goes entirely to state and city government rather than into your account.
